advances: Proves the unconditional scalar estimate \(K(w)\ge W/[24(n+1)2^n]\) using comparable-weight bands defined relative to the maximum in each parity class. A direct probability-domination depth lemma gives the stronger actual-body transfer \(h_{\max}(C)\ge K(w)/12\). Their composition supplies one point of mixed-integer depth at least \(W/[288(n+1)2^n]\), uniformly in the continuous dimension. The coefficient still depends on the integer dimension through \(1/(n+1)\), so this is not a final proof of the locked conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources:
The log-concave centroid input is the exact statement already recorded in accepted fact `5bd39b316ef3c194`. It was also checked in the author-hosted primary manuscript of László Lovász and Santosh Vempala, [The Geometry of Logconcave Functions and Sampling Algorithms](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~vempala/papers/logcon.pdf), Lemma 5.12, printed page 24; [journal DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/rsa.20135). In exact mathematical form: for a log-concave probability density \(g\) with centroid \(c=\int xg(x)\,dx\), every halfspace \(H\ni c\) satisfies \(\int_Hg\ge1/e\). The conditional densities in (10) are normalized, log-concave, and compactly supported, so their centroids exist; their conditioning sets may be open. The same manuscript's Theorem 5.1, printed page 14, states the convolution closure used for the two uniform probability densities defining \(\nu_0\), as already recorded in `03f650d1c4f1b86d` and `280b299bc1e87c14`.

The Brunn-Minkowski premise is used through its exact statement in `03f650d1c4f1b86d`: for nonempty bounded measurable sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^d\) and \(0<t<1\) with measurable Minkowski sum, \(\operatorname{vol}_d((1-t)A+tB)^{1/d}\ge(1-t)\operatorname{vol}_d(A)^{1/d}+t\operatorname{vol}_d(B)^{1/d}\). Here the sets to which it is applied are positive-volume compact convex fibers or reflected intersections, their sums are compact, and the required containments are proved in (12) and (14). Empty and zero-volume intersections are handled separately. No computational or unaccepted research assertion is a premise.
proof:
We first prove the scalar assertion. The positive support is finite and nonempty. Every \(\mathcal U_j\) is finite, even, and contains zero. The midpoint hypothesis gives \(\Delta_j(v)\ge0\); also \(\Delta_j(0)=0\) and \(\alpha(0)=w_j\). All curvatures are finite on their stated domains. For any \(L\ge0\), the largest curvature value \(t\le L\) at the fixed center exists because zero is one such value. The cutoff sums at \(t\) and \(L\) agree, while \(1+t\le1+L\). Hence the maximum defining \(K_j(w)\) is attained at a member of the finite set \(\{\Delta_j(v):v\in\mathcal U_j\}\). Finiteness of the positive support gives attainment of \(K(w)\). This is the same finite-cutoff argument as in `997f7c3a0c4804e4`.

For each parity class \(b\in(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n\) containing positive weight, choose \(a_b\equiv b\pmod2\) with maximal weight in that class and put \(m_b:=w_{a_b}>0\). For every positive \(z\equiv b\pmod2\), the midpoint hypothesis gives \(w_{(z+a_b)/2}\ge\sqrt{m_bw_z}\). For fixed \(b\), the map \(z\mapsto(z+a_b)/2\) is injective and takes values in \(\mathbb Z^n\). All its images have positive weights. Consequently,

\[
\sum_{\substack{z\equiv b\pmod2\\w_z>0}}\sqrt{m_bw_z}
\le\sum_{\substack{z\equiv b\pmod2\\w_z>0}}w_{(z+a_b)/2}
\le W.
\tag{5}
\]

When \(0<w_z\le4^{-(n+1)}m_b\), one has \(\sqrt{m_bw_z}\ge2^{n+1}w_z\). Thus the total weight at such sites in this class is at most \(2^{-(n+1)}W\). Summing this estimate over at most \(2^n\) nonempty parity classes shows that the sites satisfying \(w_z>4^{-(n+1)}m_b\) in their own class carry at least \(W/2\). Images used in (5) need be distinct only within each fixed class; the last summation uses the separate upper bounds and makes no cross-class injectivity assertion.

For every nonempty class \(b\) and integer \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), define

\[
A_{b,k}:=\{z\equiv b\pmod2:4^{-(k+1)}m_b<w_z\le4^{-k}m_b\},
\qquad U_{b,k}:=\sum_{z\in A_{b,k}}w_z.
\]

The strict lower and weak upper inequalities partition all the retained positive sites, including any sites lying exactly on a band endpoint. There are at most \(2^n(n+1)\) groups, and any two weights in the same group have ratio at most four. Including empty groups if necessary, Cauchy-Schwarz gives

\[
\sum_{b,k}U_{b,k}^2
\ge\frac{(\sum_{b,k}U_{b,k})^2}{2^n(n+1)}
\ge\frac{W^2}{4\,2^n(n+1)}.
\tag{6}
\]

Let \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band}}\) be the set of ordered pairs \((x,y)\) whose endpoints belong to the same \(A_{b,k}\), including diagonal pairs. Define the restricted score

\[
F_j^{\mathrm{band}}:=\frac1{w_j}
\sum_{\substack{(x,y)\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band}}\\x+y=2j}}w_xw_y
\qquad(w_j>0).
\]

This is the quantity denoted \(F_j\) in the supplied parity-local-band response. The label \(F_j\) remains reserved here for the all-pair score \(w_j^{-1}\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}w_{j+v}w_{j-v}\) of `997f7c3a0c4804e4`; the exact relation is \(0\le F_j^{\mathrm{band}}\le F_j\), not equality in general. The restriction does not change the endpoint-to-displacement normalization: \((x,y)\mapsto(j,v)=((x+y)/2,(x-y)/2)\) is the same bijection on the selected pairs. Every selected pair has a positive integer midpoint, so

\[
\sum_{j:w_j>0}w_jF_j^{\mathrm{band}}
=\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band}}}w_xw_y
=\sum_{b,k}U_{b,k}^2.
\tag{7}
\]

For two independent sites sampled with probabilities \(w_z/W\), the probability that both belong to the same retained band is exactly \(\sum_{b,k}(U_{b,k}/W)^2\). Thus (7) keeps the original total-weight normalization, including the discarded tail in \(W\). Taking the weighted average with probabilities \(w_j/W\), choose one positive center \(j\) with \(F_j^{\mathrm{band}}\ge W/[4\,2^n(n+1)]\). Fix it for the rest of the scalar proof. Each contributing displacement satisfies

\[
\frac{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}{w_j}
=\sqrt{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}\,e^{-\Delta_j(v)/2}
\le2\alpha(v)e^{-\Delta_j(v)/2}.
\tag{8}
\]

Indeed, if the smaller endpoint weight is \(a>0\), the larger is at most \(4a\), so their geometric mean is at most \(2a\). Enlarge the resulting nonnegative sum to all of \(\mathcal U_j\). Using the discounted score \(E_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\alpha(v)e^{-\Delta_j(v)/2}\), with exactly the exponent and normalization of `c382ad0f37a86dd8`, we obtain \(F_j^{\mathrm{band}}\le2E_j\). This discounted score is distinct from the entropy quantity named \(E_j\) in `03f650d1c4f1b86d`; only that predecessor's geometric and density statements are used below. The following proof of the cutoff bound needs only the midpoint hypothesis used here:

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_j
&=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\alpha(v)
  \int_{\Delta_j(v)}^\infty\tfrac12e^{-s/2}\,ds\\
&=\int_0^\infty\tfrac12e^{-s/2}B_j^\Delta(s)\,ds\\
&\le K_j(w)\int_0^\infty\tfrac12e^{-s/2}(1+s)\,ds
=3K_j(w).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

The sum is finite, the two moments in the last integral are one and two, and the integral starting at zero equals one. Thus the diagonal contribution and all curvature-zero pairs are counted exactly. Combining (6)--(9) yields \(K(w)\ge K_j(w)\ge F_j^{\mathrm{band}}/6\ge W/[24(n+1)2^n]\), proving (1).

We next prove (2). Domination gives \(\nu\ll Q\ll\operatorname{vol}_d\), and \(\operatorname{supp}\nu\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q\), so \(\nu\) has compact support and every affine hyperplane is \(\nu\)-null. For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}\), put \(G(x,u):=\{y:u^\top(y-x)\ge0\}\). Every proper closed halfspace containing \(x\) contains one of these through-point halfspaces. If \((x_k,u_k)\to(x,u)\), the indicators of \(G(x_k,u_k)\) converge to that of \(G(x,u)\) outside its boundary hyperplane. Dominated convergence therefore shows that \((x,u)\mapsto\nu(G(x,u))\) is continuous.

The sphere is compact, so \(\operatorname{TD}_\nu(x)=\min_{u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}}\nu(G(x,u))\). Uniform continuity on the product of any compact neighborhood of \(x\) with the sphere shows that this minimum is continuous in \(x\). The convex hull of the nonempty compact support is compact in finite-dimensional space. Strict separation gives depth zero at every point outside that convex hull. Nonnegativity and continuity consequently imply that \(\delta:=\sup_x\operatorname{TD}_\nu(x)\) is attained on \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}\nu)\). This argument uses absolute continuity of \(\nu\), and does not require a continuous density version for \(\nu\).

Suppose for contradiction that \(\delta<1/[6(1+L)]\), and set \(r:=\lceil3(1+L)\rceil\). Then \(3(1+L)\le r\le4(1+L)\), so \(1-r\delta>1/3\). We construct open convex remainders \(D_0,\ldots,D_r\), beginning with \(D_0=\mathbb R^d\). Inductively suppose \(i<r\) and \(\nu(D_i)\ge1-i\delta\). This is greater than \(1/3\), so domination gives \(Q(D_i)\ge e^{-L}\nu(D_i)>0\). If \(g\) is the log-concave density of \(Q\), its conditional law on \(D_i\) has density \(g_i:=g\mathbf1_{D_i}/Q(D_i)\). The indicator of an open convex set is log-concave with the zero-outside convention, hence so is \(g_i\). It integrates to one and has a finite first absolute moment, because the reference has compact support. Thus its centroid \(c_i:=\int y g_i(y)\,dy\) is defined.

Choose a minimizing direction for \(\operatorname{TD}_\nu(c_i)\) and let \(H_i\) be that closed halfspace through \(c_i\). Then \(\nu(H_i)=\operatorname{TD}_\nu(c_i)\le\delta\). The centroid need not lie in \(\operatorname{supp}\nu\); this inequality uses the global supremum \(\delta\). The exact log-concave centroid inequality recorded in the external-sources statement and proof of accepted fact `5bd39b316ef3c194` gives \(\int_{H_i}g_i\ge1/e>1/3\). Its hypotheses are precisely normalization, log-concavity, an existing centroid, and a halfspace containing it. They hold for this open-set conditioning; no closed-support or density-continuity hypothesis is needed.

Set \(D_{i+1}:=D_i\setminus H_i\). This is the intersection of \(D_i\) with an open halfspace and is again open and convex. Directly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu(D_{i+1})
&\ge\nu(D_i)-\nu(H_i)\ge1-(i+1)\delta,\\
Q(D_{i+1})
&=Q(D_i)\left(1-\int_{H_i}g_i\right)
\le\tfrac23Q(D_i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]

The lower bound stays greater than \(1/3\) through \(i+1=r\), so every conditioning required by the induction has positive mass. The measures \(\nu\), \(Q\), and all conditional reference laws are absolutely continuous; consequently all cutting hyperplanes are null. The set difference and the identities in (10) also account explicitly for the use of closed cutting halfspaces and open remainders.

At the end \(\nu(D_r)>1/3\) and \(Q(D_r)\le(2/3)^r\). Domination gives the incompatible bound

\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu(D_r)
&\le e^LQ(D_r)
\le e^L(2/3)^r\\
&\le e^L(2/3)^{3(1+L)}
=\frac8{27}\left(\frac{8e}{27}\right)^L
\le\frac8{27}<\frac13.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

The elementary inequality \(e<3\) gives both \(1/e>1/3\) above and \(8e/27<1\) here. For example, its exponential series gives \(e=1+1+\sum_{k\ge2}1/k!<2+\sum_{k\ge2}2^{-(k-1)}=3\). Thus the contradiction proves the lower bound for the attained \(\delta\), establishing (2).

Now let \(C\) be the actual body with \(W>0\). Its compact base projection contains only finitely many lattice points, so its volume table is finite. If two endpoint fibers have positive volume, each is a full-dimensional compact convex set. Their Minkowski average is contained in the intermediate fiber by convexity of \(C\), and contains a ball of positive radius. In particular that intermediate fiber has positive volume. The Brunn-Minkowski inequality in the precise form recorded in `03f650d1c4f1b86d` gives, for same-parity positive integer endpoints \(x,y\),

\[
w_{(x+y)/2}^{1/d}
\ge\frac{w_x^{1/d}+w_y^{1/d}}2
\ge(w_xw_y)^{1/(2d)}.
\tag{12}
\]

The last inequality is the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Raising to the power \(2d\) proves the required scalar hypothesis, with the exact actual weights and all zero-volume fibers retained as zeros. The midpoint in (12) is an integer by the parity condition.

Fix a positive center \(j\). To check the density comparison independently, take \(v\in\mathcal U_j\) and independent uniform samples from its two endpoint fibers. Convolution of their normalized indicator densities, followed by the change of variables from the sum to half the sum, gives

\[
f_v(x)
=\frac{2^d}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbf1_{C_{j+v}}(y)\mathbf1_{C_{j-v}}(2x-y)\,dy
=\frac{2^d\operatorname{vol}_d R_v(x)}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}.
\tag{13}
\]

This formula has total integral one by that change of variables and Tonelli's theorem. It is continuous: the boundary of a positive-volume compact convex set is Lebesgue-null, so for \(x_k\to x\), the second indicator converges for almost every \(y\), while the first indicator is an integrable dominating function. To recall why that boundary is null, contraction about an interior point by a factor \(1-\varepsilon\) lies in the interior, and the volume difference from the original body is \([1-(1-\varepsilon)^d]\) times its volume, tending to zero. This bounds the boundary volume by a quantity tending to zero. Moreover, all midpoint samples lie in \(C_j\), which is compact, so each law is supported there.

Reflection gives \(R_{-v}(x)=2x-R_v(x)\), with equal volumes. If \(p\in R_v(x)\) and \(q\in R_{-v}(x)\), then \(p,2x-q\in C_{j+v}\) and \(q,2x-p\in C_{j-v}\). Applying convexity of the same body to these two endpoint pairs shows that both \((p+q)/2\) and \(2x-(p+q)/2\) lie in \(C_j\). Therefore

\[
\frac{R_v(x)+R_{-v}(x)}2\subseteq R_0(x).
\tag{14}
\]

If \(R_v(x)\) has positive volume, it and its reflection are nonempty compact convex sets, and Brunn-Minkowski in the same accepted form gives \(\operatorname{vol}_d R_0(x)\ge\operatorname{vol}_d R_v(x)\). If \(R_v(x)\) is empty or has zero volume, this inequality follows from nonnegativity without applying Brunn-Minkowski. Substituting it into (13) gives the pointwise comparison

\[
f_v(x)\le\frac{w_j^2}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}f_0(x)
=e^{\Delta_j(v)}f_0(x)
\quad(x\in\mathbb R^d).
\tag{15}
\]

In particular, a zero value of \(f_0\) forces a zero value of every \(f_v\), and integration gives \(\nu_v\ll\nu_0\) with the stated bounded density ratio. This rederives the exact comparison of `280b299bc1e87c14`, before any coarser replacement by minimum endpoint volume.

The normalized indicator of \(C_j\) is log-concave. The convolution-closure theorem, recorded in `03f650d1c4f1b86d` and applied to this exact central law in `280b299bc1e87c14`, makes its self-convolution log-concave. An invertible linear change of variables and a positive normalization preserve log-concavity. Thus \(Q=\nu_0\) has the required log-concave density \(f_0\), compactly supported in \(C_j\).

Fix a cutoff \(L\ge0\) and use the specified even thinning \(q_v\). Its mass is \(M_q=B_j^\Delta(L)\ge w_j>0\), because zero is retained. The finite mixture \(P_{j,q}\) is a probability measure supported in \(C_j\). Equation (15), multiplied by its nonnegative mixture weights and summed only over \(\Delta_j(v)\le L\), proves \(P_{j,q}\le e^LQ\) on every Borel set. Apply (2) with its \(\nu=P_{j,q}\) and \(Q=\nu_0\). It provides \(x_{j,L}^\star\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}P_{j,q})\subseteq C_j\), fixed before any halfspace, such that \(\operatorname{TD}_{P_{j,q}}(x_{j,L}^\star)\ge1/[6(1+L)]\).

We prove the mixed-volume lift at this same point directly. Write \(p=(j,x_{j,L}^\star)\) and take any proper closed ambient halfspace through \(p\), in the form

\[
H=\{(z,y):a^\top(z-j)+b^\top(y-x_{j,L}^\star)\ge0\},
\qquad(a,b)\ne(0,0).
\]

For each integer \(z\), put \(H_z:=\{y:(z,y)\in H\}\). If \(b\ne0\), let \(G:=\{y:b^\top(y-x_{j,L}^\star)\ge0\}\); if \(b=0\), let \(G:=\mathbb R^d\). In either case \(H_j=G\). For a reflected pair of independent endpoint samples, the two ambient affine scores sum to \(2b^\top((X^++X^-)/2-x_{j,L}^\star)\). If its midpoint belongs to \(G\), that sum is nonnegative, so at least one endpoint belongs to its ambient halfspace section. The assertion also holds when \(b=0\), when the sum is identically zero. The union bound consequently gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha(v)\nu_v(G)
&\le\alpha(v)\bigl(\lambda_{j+v}(H_{j+v})+\lambda_{j-v}(H_{j-v})\bigr)\\
&\le\operatorname{vol}_d(C_{j+v}\cap H_{j+v})
   +\operatorname{vol}_d(C_{j-v}\cap H_{j-v}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]

The last step uses \(\alpha(v)\le w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\). For the central displacement, applying the same union bound to two independent samples from \(\lambda_j\) gives

\[
\frac{w_j}{2}\nu_0(G)
\le w_j\lambda_j(G)
=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_j\cap H_j).
\tag{17}
\]

Choose one representative of each unordered pair \(\{v,-v\}\) of retained nonzero displacements. The two orientations have identical coefficients and midpoint laws. Distinct unordered pairs have disjoint endpoint fibers, since an equality \(j\pm v=j\pm v'\) implies \(v'=v\) or \(v'=-v\). None of those endpoint fibers is central. Summing (16) once per representative and adding (17), while retaining the nonnegative contributions of all other fibers, therefore gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)
&\ge\frac12\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}q_v\nu_v(G)\\
&=\frac{B_j^\Delta(L)}2P_{j,q}(G)
\ge\frac{B_j^\Delta(L)}{12(1+L)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{18}
\]

When \(b\ne0\), the last inequality is the depth guarantee for the closed halfspace \(G\) containing \(x_{j,L}^\star\). When \(b=0\), it follows from \(P_{j,q}(G)=1\). In that vertical case, \(H_j=\mathbb R^d\): the entire central fiber is on the ambient boundary and is included with full volume in (17). For a noncentral pair with \(a^\top v=0\), both endpoint fibers are on that boundary and are included as well. All implications in (16)--(18) use weak inequalities, so they do not assume that ambient boundary hyperplanes have zero mixed volume.

Every proper closed halfspace containing \(p\) contains a parallel through-\(p\) halfspace. Monotonicity extends (18) to all such halfspaces. If the whole space is admitted, its mass \(W\) also suffices: injectivity of \(v\mapsto j+v\) and \(\alpha(v)\le w_{j+v}\) give \(B_j^\Delta(L)\le W\). Taking the infimum proves (3).

The scalar attainment argument gives a center and finite cutoff maximizing \(B_j^\Delta(L)/(1+L)\). Choose these first and then the probability-depth point just constructed. Formula (3) gives a single \(p^\star\) with \(h_S(p^\star)\ge K(w)/12\); inserting (1) gives (4). The center, cutoff, and continuous point are all fixed before the ambient halfspace.

For completeness, the maximum defining \(h_{\max}(C)\) exists even though mixed volume can charge ambient hyperplanes. Extend mixed volume on \(S\) to a finite Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^{n+d}\) by summing volume on its finitely many fibers. For a fixed unit ambient normal \(u\), the function \(p\mapsto\mu(\{q:u^\top(q-p)\ge0\})\) is upper semicontinuous. Indeed, for \(p_k\to p\), the pointwise upper limit of these halfspace indicators is at most the limiting closed-halfspace indicator, and the reverse Fatou inequality for a finite measure gives the same upper-limit inequality for their integrals. The depth is the infimum of these upper semicontinuous functions over unit normals, hence is upper semicontinuous. The set \(S\) is nonempty and compact, so it attains its maximum there. This does not require absolute continuity of the ambient mixed measure.

Finally, if \(W=0\), every closed-halfspace intersection has nonnegative mixed volume and the asserted lower bound is zero. Any point in \(S\) works. For \(W>0\), the coefficient in (4) equals \(1/[288(n+1)]\) times \(2^{-n}\) and tends to zero as \(n\) grows, leaving the absolute-constant requirement in the locked problem unresolved.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, let \(w=(w_z)_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\) be a nonzero, nonnegative, finitely supported table of finite real numbers, and put \(W:=\sum_z w_z>0\). Assume the same-parity midpoint hypothesis of accepted fact `997f7c3a0c4804e4`: whenever \(x,y\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfy \(x\equiv y\pmod2\) and \(w_xw_y>0\), one has \(w_{(x+y)/2}^2\ge w_xw_y\). Congruence is coordinatewise. No global log-concave extension of the table is assumed.

For each \(j\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(w_j>0\), retain \(\alpha(v):=\min\{w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\}\), \(\mathcal U_j:=\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:\alpha(v)>0\}\), and \(\Delta_j(v):=\log(w_j^2/(w_{j+v}w_{j-v}))\) for \(v\in\mathcal U_j\). All logarithms are natural. The dependence of \(\alpha\) on the fixed center is suppressed, exactly as in accepted facts `280b299bc1e87c14` and `997f7c3a0c4804e4`; it is the displayed-center \(\alpha_j\) of accepted fact `c382ad0f37a86dd8`. Retain their cutoff and score definitions

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_j^\Delta(L)&:=\sum_{\substack{v\in\mathcal U_j\\\Delta_j(v)\le L}}\alpha(v)
&& (L\ge0),\\
K_j(w)&:=\max_{L\ge0}\frac{B_j^\Delta(L)}{1+L},
&K(w)&:=\max_{j:w_j>0}K_j(w).
\end{aligned}
\]

Every displacement sum is oriented and includes zero. These maxima are attained, and there exists a positive center \(j\) such that \(K_j(w)\ge W/[24(n+1)2^n]\). In particular,

\[
K(w)\ge\frac{W}{24(n+1)2^n}.
\tag{1}
\]

The probability ingredient has the following independent scope. For an integer \(d\ge1\), let \(Q\) be a compactly supported Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\) having a measurable log-concave Lebesgue density. Let \(\nu\) be a Borel probability measure such that \(\nu(A)\le e^LQ(A)\) for every Borel set \(A\), where \(L\ge0\). For any finite measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), put \(\operatorname{TD}_\mu(x):=\inf_{G\ni x}\mu(G)\), over proper closed halfspaces \(G\subset\mathbb R^d\), as in `280b299bc1e87c14`. Then \(\nu\) is absolutely continuous, its depth is continuous, and its maximum is attained at some \(x^\star\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}\nu)\), with

\[
\operatorname{TD}_\nu(x^\star)
=\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\operatorname{TD}_\nu(x)
\ge\frac1{6(1+L)}.
\tag{2}
\]

Here \(Q\) denotes a probability measure, not a quadratic form. In the application below it is exactly the central midpoint law \(\nu_0\).

For that application, let \(n,d\ge1\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, and suppose \(S:=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\ne\varnothing\). Give \(C_z:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:(z,x)\in C\}\), \(w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\), \(W:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}w_z=\mathcal H_d(S)\), and \(h_S(p):=\inf_{H\ni p}\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\) their exact meanings in `280b299bc1e87c14`. Empty and lower-dimensional fibers have zero volume; \(H\) ranges over closed ambient halfspaces. The quantity \(h_{\max}(C):=\max_{p\in S}h_S(p)\) is attained.

Assume first that \(W>0\). The actual volume table satisfies the scalar hypotheses. For every positive center \(j\) and \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), let \(\lambda_{j+v}\) and \(\lambda_{j-v}\) be uniform probability laws on the positive-volume endpoint fibers, and let \(\nu_v\) be the law of the midpoint of independent samples from them. These are exactly the midpoint laws of `280b299bc1e87c14` and `03f650d1c4f1b86d`; \(\nu_0\) uses two independent samples from \(C_j\), and \(\nu_v=\nu_{-v}\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), put \(R_v(x):=C_{j+v}\cap(2x-C_{j-v})\). The continuous density versions

\[
f_v(x):=\frac{2^d\operatorname{vol}_d R_v(x)}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}
\]

satisfy \(f_v(x)\le e^{\Delta_j(v)}f_0(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), including points where \(f_0(x)=0\). The reference \(Q=\nu_0\) has a log-concave density and is supported in \(C_j\).
